sections.overview: The Eurasian oystercatcher is a large, stocky black-and-white wader that is a familiar sight on shores and estuaries. It is also an adaptable bird: over the last fifty years some have begun to breed inland, even on urban rooftops.
sections.identification: The plumage is black and white, with a long orange-red bill and pinkish-red legs. In flight it shows a broad white wing stripe, a black tail and a white rump that extends in a V between the wings. In British BTO data, females and males have similar measurements: mean mass 549 vs 544 g and wing length 264 vs 263 mm, respectively.
sections.habitat: In Britain breeding birds are most frequent on estuaries and also common on open shore, but many nest inland, especially in northern Britain, along rivers and in wet meadows. In winter it occupies rocky and estuarine shores, with the largest concentrations on major estuaries.
sections.diet: It eats cockles and mussels, which it prises open or hammers open with its strong bill. In winter on The Wash, birds rely heavily on cockles and blue mussels.
sections.behavior: From autumn, oystercatchers gather in large flocks along the shore, and on the British east coast resident birds are joined by others from Norway. Morecambe Bay holds the most wintering birds in the UK, about 40,000 counted at high-tide roosts in a recent winter. Ringing shows little exchange between the Atlantic and continental populations.
sections.reproduction: In Britain the average first clutch date is 19 May. The typical clutch is two or three eggs, incubated by both sexes for 24–27 days. The chicks are downy and active from hatching and fledge after 34–37 days. There is one brood a year, and breeding typically starts at age four.
sections.ecology: Because it eats cockles, the oystercatcher is vulnerable where cockle beds are overfished. In the Netherlands, shellfisheries have been linked to lower winter survival. Inland, a 95% decline between 1990 and 2015 at one Perthshire study site was attributed to land-use change.
sections.conservation: The IUCN lists it as Near Threatened globally, and it is Amber-listed in the UK. The UK breeding population was 96,000 pairs in 2016 and fell by 23% between 1995 and 2024; the main causes of the recent decline are unclear. A bird that reaches breeding age lives about 12 years; the oldest ringed bird passed 41.
